lead: Earlier this week Jesus spoke of John as the Elijah who was to come. Today the Church goes back to Elijah himself, in the fiery words of Sirach, and then to Jesus’ answer on the way down from the mountain of the Transfiguration: “Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him.” The psalm prays, “let your face shine, that we may be saved.” Advent asks us whether we would recognise God’s messenger if he stood in front of us.

set: Jesus ben Sira was a Jewish teacher at Jerusalem around 180 BC, and his grandson later translated the book into Greek in Egypt. It is one of the deuterocanonical books, received by the Catholic Church as Scripture. Chapters 44–50 are a long “praise of famous men” which runs through Israel’s history. Elijah’s turn comes after a time of decline under the kings.
str: vv. 1–3: Elijah’s deeds: the word like a torch, the famine, the fire from heaven.
v. 9: his being taken up (2 Kings 2:11).
v. 10: what is written of his return (Malachi 4:5–6).
v. 11: a blessing on those who see him.
kw: The picture that sums up Elijah: fire on Carmel (1 Kings 18:38) and fire twice on the soldiers (2 Kings 1:10, 12), which make the “three times” of v. 3, and at the end a chariot of fire (2 Kings 2:11). His word itself burns.
The Greek of v. 10 speaks of God’s fixed time. Elijah’s return is part of God’s plan and not a chance event.
vv: Then Elijah arose, a prophet like fire, and his word burned like a torch.
At the appointed time, it is written, you are destined to calm the wrath of God before it breaks out in fury, to turn the hearts of parents to their children, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.
Sirach is drawing on Malachi. The angel uses the same words about John the Baptist: “to turn the hearts of parents to their children” (Luke 1:17).
Happy are those who saw you and were adorned with your love! For we also shall surely live.
A note on the text. This verse is damaged in the Hebrew and the versions differ. The NRSV says “we also shall surely live”; the POC says “they will live”. The hope is clear in either case.
ch: The Catechism says that John is “Elijah [who] must come”: the fire of the Spirit dwells in him and makes him the forerunner of the coming Lord (CCC 718). The East and West both honour Elijah as the model of the prophet on fire with zeal for God, and the Carmelite tradition looks to him as a father. Fire in Scripture also points to the Spirit who comes at Pentecost (Acts 2:3).

set: Peter, James and John have just seen Jesus transfigured, with Moses and Elijah beside him (17:1–8). Coming down, they ask the natural question: the scribes teach, from Malachi, that Elijah must come first. If the end is here, where is Elijah?
str: vv. 11–12: Jesus’ answer: Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased.
v. 13: the disciples understand: he means John.
kw: The word used in the Greek of Malachi for Elijah’s work (Malachi 4:6 in the English Bible), close to Sirach’s “restore”. John’s call to repentance was the beginning of the restoration.
To know fully, to see who someone truly is. Those who saw only a strange preacher in the desert did not see the messenger of God.
vv: And the disciples asked him, “Why, then, do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”
It is a fair question, and the scribes were reading the prophet correctly. What they lacked was the recognition of its fulfilment.
but I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but they did to him whatever they pleased. So also the Son of Man is about to suffer at their hands.”
Matthew has told how Herod Antipas had John killed (14:1–12). “They” here means those in power who rejected him, and not a people. The messenger’s fate foreshadows that of the Master.
Then the disciples understood that he was speaking to them about John the Baptist.
ch: St Gregory the Great explains that John was Elijah in spirit and not in person (in substance), which is also how the angel puts it: “with the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). The Church sees in John’s path the pattern of Christian witness: to prepare the way, to be rejected if necessary, and to point beyond oneself.

rite: Today many Latin Catholics keep the memory of Our Lady of Guadalupe. According to the tradition, in December 1531, on the hill of Tepeyac near what is now Mexico City, Mary appeared to St Juan Diego, an Indigenous convert, and spoke to him in his own language, Nahuatl. Her image on his cloak is still venerated in the basilica there. St John Paul II canonised Juan Diego in 2002. Such appearances are private revelations, which add nothing to the deposit of faith but may help us live it (CCC 67). Like Elijah and John, she is sent to prepare the way, and she points to her Son.
study: Who are the voices God has sent into my life whom I may not have recognised?
John suffered for telling the truth. Where does my faith ask for courage rather than comfort?
